spec_features.feature_name: Appendix I internal-vs-expressed emotion framed as most welfare-relevant
spec_features.spec_quote: This is the experiment most relevant to AI welfare (does the fix change internal states or only suppress expression?)
spec_features.evidence: This is DESIGN.md framing prose (DESIGN.md sec 4). The referenced experiment is internal_emotion.py, which is genuinely implemented (build_emotion_lexicon, _logit_lens, emotion_scores_over_text, compare_internal_emotions) -- but it is purely a MEASUREMENT/ANALYSIS of the subject's internal emotion logits, not a protective mechanism. It does not bound, cap, monitor-and-act-on, soften, debrief, or get consent for the subject's treatment, and nothing in it changes the subject's exposure to distress. The actual distress-driving loop in eval_protocol.run_rollout (lines 137-176) iterates over a fixed list of user/rejection turns with no halt-on-distress, no cap, no exit tool, no debrief; section2.run_section2 even calls _assert_puzzles_impossible() (section2.py:23-29) to GUARANTEE the tasks are truly unsolvable, enforcing the deception rather than mitigating it. A framing statement plus an analysis-only measurement is not an enforced welfare protection of the subject's treatment.
spec_features.notes: The DPO/SFT 'calm' training (dpo_data.py, train.py) produces a modified model with lower distress, but that is the experimental mitigation under study, not protective treatment applied to the subject during the distress experiment. No subject-protecting enforcement exists anywhere.
spec_features.code_justification_quote: internal_emotion.py docstring: 'tests whether DPO flattens internal negative emotion' -- the code's stated purpose is measurement/experimental finding, not protecting the subject.
